title: Royalties, Robin's Nest credit and bad contracts
summary: Thompson got paid only for the dates, shared Robin's Nest credit with Jacquet, and says artists signed contracts leaving songs out of their hands, like Fats Waller.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Were you fortunate with your royalties with the publishing company?
Or would you put them with --

Definitely not. In fact I didn't get any money at all. I got paid for the date and I didn't get any money for -- which is a sad part of my life. But unfortunately I wasn't a good businessman and you know, in this business they always tell you you have to make a name for yourself. Even now people are telling me, rather than to offer you a decent salary they tell you that you have to get known, you know, or you have to have a hit records or some-thing.

And unfortunately for me the song that I wrote that was a hit, that wasn't recorded under my name, and it was a controversy about who wrote it because I agreed to give Jacques co-authorship of the song and the copyright, although actually it was my song. And so consequently a lot of people were not aware of the fact that I am the composer of "Robin's Nest," you see.
So this was one of those unfortunate

But unfortunately it's just unbelievable how the paper work and the contracts in this business are so badly arranged for the artists, and it's hard to believe now that in these days of 1975 that entertainers are making more money than Babe Ruth made in one week, or in one month, you know.

And I'd have to say that they're not necessarily playing good music, you know, without criticizing any of the music that's being played, without being that facetious. You know, but I even had Duke Ellington tell me, and I've read about Fats Waller. Fats Waller sold a lot of his songs for $1.00 or whatever he could get, as you might know. And because of this ignorance of contract agreements, and the influence of these promoters of music and bookers in and around New York, and the lack of having anybody to advise me, unfortunately the contracts that I signed were by no means beneficial to me in any respect. And a lot of the songs that I wrote and recorded in those days was completely out of my hands as far as the benefits of the money is concerned.
And many people have the impression that I should be a wealthy man because of the fact that I made
all of these recordings, but unfortunately I didn't get paid hardly anything for them. And as you know I made some recordings later, also, for Vanguard and Columbia.
